project.name: tinyshop
project.one_liner: A three-product shop: a JSON API in plain Python and a one-page web front end.
project.what: tinyshop sells tea, a mug and a kettle. The browser page lists the products and posts orders to a small Python server, which prices them and saves them to a JSON file. It exists to show the smallest complete web app: a catalog, a write path and storage.
project.analogy: A market stall with a price list on the counter and a notebook for orders. The stall keeper (the server) checks every item against the price list before writing the order down.
project.audience: Developers learning how a front end, an API and storage fit together.

lessons.title: What tinyshop is
lessons.summary: A browser page lists three products and sends orders to a Python server, which prices them and saves them to a file.
lessons.body:
There are two halves. The **web page** in `web/` shows the catalog and a Buy button. The **server** in `app/` answers two questions: what can I buy ([[app/server.py:17-21|def do_GET]]) and please place this order ([[app/server.py:23-32|def do_POST]]).

Orders are written to a JSON file so they survive a restart ([[app/store.py:40-42|def _save]]).

checkpoint.q: Where does an order end up after you click Buy?
choices: In a JSON file written by the server
checkpoint.explain: The store appends the order and calls `_save`, which writes every order to the JSON file: [[app/store.py:36-37|self._save()]].

lessons.title: Run it on your machine
lessons.summary: Start the server with one Python command, then open the web page.
lessons.body: Nothing to install: the server only uses the standard library ([[app/server.py:1-2|from http.server import]]). Run it as a module so its relative imports work, then open `web/index.html`.

lessons.title: Python's built-in web server
lessons.summary: `http.server` turns a class with `do_GET` and `do_POST` methods into a web server.
lessons.body: Each request creates a `Handler` ([[app/server.py:9|class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler)]]). Python calls `do_GET` or `do_POST` depending on the HTTP method, and the method writes the response itself.

lessons.title: The map: two folders, three layers
lessons.summary: The page talks to the HTTP layer, the HTTP layer talks to the store, and the store owns the data.
lessons.body: `web/app.js` only knows URLs ([[web/app.js:1|const API]]). `app/server.py` only knows the store ([[app/server.py:6|store = Store()]]). `app/store.py` is the only code that touches the catalog and the file.

lessons.title: Prices are whole cents
lessons.summary: Money is stored as an integer number of cents so totals never pick up rounding errors.
lessons.body: A product's price is `price_cents`, an integer ([[app/models.py:6-9|price_cents: int]]). The page divides by 100 only when it displays the total ([[web/app.js:17|order.total_cents / 100]]).

lessons.title: What happens when you click Buy
lessons.summary: The page posts the checked SKUs, the server prices them, the store saves the order and the page shows the total.
lessons.body: Follow one click from the button to the file and back. Use the step-through below; each step opens the real code.

checkpoint.q: A customer posts an unknown SKU. What do they get back?
checkpoint.explain: `place_order` raises `KeyError`, and `do_POST` turns it into a 400: [[app/server.py:30-31|except KeyError as exc]].

lessons.title: Products, orders and the JSON file
lessons.summary: Two dataclasses describe the data; orders persist as a JSON list.
lessons.body: The catalog is a constant list in code ([[app/store.py:6-10|CATALOG = []]). Orders load from the file when the store starts ([[app/store.py:20-24|def _load]]).

lessons.title: The files worth opening
lessons.summary: Five files hold the whole app; start with the store.
lessons.body: Read them in this order: store, server, page script, models, test.

lessons.title: Build it again, in order
lessons.summary: Models first, then the store, then the server, then the page.
lessons.body: Each layer only depends on the one below it, so you can build and test them bottom-up.

lessons.title: Why a JSON file and not a database
lessons.summary: A file keeps the example dependency-free; it would not survive two servers writing at once.
lessons.body: The whole order list is rewritten on every order ([[app/store.py:40-42|json.dump]]). That is simple and fine for one process.

lessons.title: Two orders at the same time
lessons.summary: Order ids come from the list length and the file is rewritten whole, so concurrent writes can collide.
lessons.body: The id is `len(self.orders) + 1` ([[app/store.py:34|Order(id=len(self.orders) + 1]]). Two servers sharing one file would hand out the same id.

lessons.title: Your first changes
lessons.summary: Add a product, then add a route that lists orders.
lessons.body: Start with the easy one; it touches a single line.

decisions.title: Orders in a JSON file
decisions.choice: Rewrite the whole list on every order.
decisions.tradeoff: Unsafe with more than one writer.

risks.title: Duplicate order ids under concurrency
risks.why: Ids come from the list length.
risks.advice: Use a counter stored with the data, or a database sequence.
